corpus_definition: to suddenly push air out through your nose and mouth

forms.definition: a sudden loud push of air out of your nose
forms.example: I heard a loud sneeze from the back of the bus.

syn.note: Related: air comes out of your mouth from the chest, not suddenly through the nose.

forms.definition: to suddenly push air out through your nose, often when ill
forms.example: Dust always makes me sneeze.

syn.note: Related body action, but from the chest and mouth.

forms.note: 'sneezy' appears only in very informal English; not a learner-dictionary word.

context.text: In spring Dilnoza sneezes all day because of the flowers. One loud sneeze in class made everyone laugh.

reviewer_note: Noun and verb are the same spelling; no other family forms exist.

corpus_definition: relating to people and how they live together in groups.

forms.definition: people living together in a country or group, with shared laws and customs
forms.example: Teachers play an important role in our society.

syn.note: A smaller group of people living in one place or sharing interests.
Related: ordinary people in general.

forms.definition: to spend time with other people in a friendly way
forms.example: After work we like to socialize in a cafe.
forms.note: British English also spells it socialise.

syn.note: Meet and talk with different people at an event.
Informal: spend free time with friends.

forms.definition: connected with people and how they live and spend time together
forms.example: Social media helps me stay in touch with friends.

syn.note: Related: about people in general, not one person.
Shared by a group of people living together.

ant.note: Not wanting to be with other people, or harmful to them.

forms.definition: friendly and enjoying being with other people
forms.example: My brother is very sociable and talks to everyone.

syn.note: Kind and pleasant to others.
Likes meeting new people.

forms.definition: connected with the whole of a country's people and their way of life
forms.example: Unemployment is a big societal problem.

forms.definition: in a way connected with meeting and being with people
forms.example: We work together, but we never meet socially.

people.definition: the study of how people live in groups
people.example: She studies sociology at university in Tashkent.

people.definition: a person who studies how groups of people live
people.example: A sociologist asked us questions about our families.

people.definition: a person who supports shared ownership of industry by the state
people.note: Belongs to social = a political system, not people spending time together.

context.text: Aziz is very sociable. He loves social events and socializes with his neighbours every evening.

reviewer_note: sociable kept as an entry (common family word), not a synonym; antisocial in ant.

corpus_definition: The dark earth on the ground where plants grow.

forms.definition: the top layer of the ground where plants grow
forms.example: Tomatoes grow well in this soil.

syn.note: Same meaning; very common in gardening.
The surface you walk on; also used for soil.
Common in American English; in British English it often means something unclean.

forms.definition: to make something dirty
forms.example: The child soiled his new shirt.
forms.note: Belongs to soil = make dirty, not the earth where plants grow. Formal.

forms.definition: dirty, especially clothes or sheets
forms.example: Put the soiled towels in the basket.

context.text: In the Fergana Valley the soil is rich and dark. Farmers there grow cotton, fruit and vegetables.

reviewer_note: Verb soil (make dirty) is a different meaning, so other_meaning.

corpus_definition: When a part of your body feels hurt.

forms.definition: a feeling of pain in a part of the body
forms.example: The soreness in my legs went away after two days.

syn.note: General word; pain can be much stronger.
A pain that goes on for some time.

forms.definition: a painful red place on the skin
forms.example: He had a small sore on his lip.

syn.note: Related: an injury that cuts the skin.

forms.definition: painful, usually because of an illness or too much use
forms.example: I have a sore throat today.

syn.note: Same meaning; easy word.
Hurting for a long time, like tired muscles.
Painful when you touch it.

forms.definition: very much, used about needing or missing something
forms.example: Help is sorely needed in the village.
forms.note: Belongs to a different sense: 'very much', not body pain. Formal.

context.text: After the football match my legs were sore. The soreness lasted until Monday.

reviewer_note: sorely is a false friend (means 'very much'), so other_meaning.

corpus_definition: to put things into groups based on their type or features

forms.definition: the work of putting things into groups
forms.example: Waste sorting is now common in many cities.

syn.note: Formal: putting things into groups by type.

forms.definition: a type or kind of person or thing
forms.example: What sort of music do you like?
forms.note: Belongs to sort = kind or type, not putting things into groups.

forms.definition: to put things into groups by type, size or colour
forms.example: Please sort the books by size.

syn.note: Put things in a clear order.
Put things in a neat or useful order.
Put things together that are similar.
Formal and scientific.

ant.note: Put different things together with no order.

forms.definition: put into groups or into the correct order
forms.example: The sorted letters are on the desk.
forms.note: In informal British English 'It's sorted' also means a problem is solved.

syn.note: In good order.

people.definition: a person or machine that puts things into groups
people.example: She works as a sorter at the post office.

context.text: At the market, Malika sorts the apples by size. The sorted apples go into different boxes.

reviewer_note: Noun sort = kind/type is a different meaning, so other_meaning; unsorted placed in ant.

corpus_definition: Having a sharp, acidic taste like a lemon.

forms.definition: a sharp taste like a lemon
forms.example: I like the sourness of green apples.

syn.note: A strong, sharp taste.
More scientific; used about food and wine.

forms.definition: to go bad and get a sharp taste, like old milk
forms.example: The milk soured in the hot kitchen.
forms.note: Also used for relationships: 'Their friendship soured.'

syn.note: British English, informal: food becomes bad.
Become bad and not safe to eat.

forms.definition: having a sharp taste like a lemon or old milk
forms.example: These cherries are too sour to eat.

syn.note: A strong taste that makes your mouth react.
More scientific word.
Pleasantly sour, used about fruit.

forms.definition: in an unfriendly or unhappy way
forms.example: 'Fine,' he said sourly.
forms.note: Belongs to sour = bad-tempered, not taste.

context.text: Grandma's green plums are very sour. I love their sourness with a little salt.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged; sourly is the bad-temper sense.

corpus_definition: a small gift bought to remember a place you visited

forms.definition: a small thing you buy to remember a place you visited
forms.example: We bought a souvenir plate in Bukhara.

syn.note: Something you keep to remember a person or event.
A small thing you keep, often a gift from someone.
Related: a souvenir is often a gift, but not always.

context.text: Tourists in Samarkand often buy a souvenir at the bazaar. A small painted plate is a popular choice.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows (A2, B1) merged; lowest level A2 used.

corpus_definition: To give money to pay for things you want or need.

forms.definition: the money that a person or government uses to buy things
forms.example: Government spending on schools went up this year.

syn.note: Formal word used in business and government.
Related: the money you have to pay.

ant.note: Keeping money instead of using it.

forms.definition: to give money to pay for things
forms.example: How much did you spend on your phone?

syn.note: Related: you pay for one thing; you spend money in general.
Informal British English: spend a lot on something nice.

forms.definition: already used, so it has no more power or use
forms.example: Throw the spent batteries away safely.
forms.note: Belongs to spend = use up, not paying money.

people.definition: a person who uses money in a certain way
people.example: My sister is a big spender when she goes shopping.

context.text: Sardor spends too much money on coffee. His mother says his spending is too high and he should save more.

reviewer_note: spent (used up) is a different sense, so other_meaning. spend time is a separate meaning not covered here.

corpus_definition: To use money to buy items or services.
particle_note: Not separable around 'on': spend + money/amount + on + thing: 'spend 50,000 som on books'. Also spend + time + on: 'spend an hour on homework'.

relations.note: Give money for one thing: 'pay for the tickets'.
Informal British English: spend a lot on something special.
Spend less money on something: 'save on electricity'.

context.text: How much do you spend on food each month? My cousin spends on clothes more than on anything else.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the example 'I love to spend on new clothes' has no money object; normally 'spend money on'.

corpus_definition: Having a strong, hot flavor from peppers or spices.

forms.definition: a powder or seed that gives food a strong taste
forms.example: Cumin is an important spice in plov.

syn.note: Anything added to food for taste, including salt.
Related: leaves of a plant used in cooking, not seeds or powder.

forms.definition: how hot and strong the taste of food is
forms.example: The spiciness of the soup surprised me.

syn.note: Used about hot food: 'I like the heat of chilli.'

forms.definition: to add powders or seeds to food for a strong taste
forms.example: She spiced the meat with black pepper.
forms.note: 'spice up' also means to make something more interesting.

syn.note: Add salt, pepper or other things to food.
British English: flavour.

forms.definition: having a strong, hot taste from peppers
forms.example: Is this sauce very spicy?

syn.note: Easy word; but hot can also mean high temperature.
Tasting strongly of pepper.
Very, very hot in taste.

ant.note: Not strong or hot in taste.

context.text: My uncle adds a lot of spice to his lagman. It is too spicy for me, but my brother loves it.

reviewer_note: spicy is made from spice, so spice is the noun main entry.
